H1.text: In a ring game, kids spin in a line, holding hands. The end kid runs. The centre kid just turns.

H2.text: Swing a cricket bat, and the tip moves faster than the handle.

H3.text: At the fair, Diya rides a merry-go-round. Her horse is near the centre. Her friend is at the edge.

H4.text: They turn together. Yet her friend rushes through the air, and Diya just drifts. How?

H5.text: The answer links two speeds: angular and linear velocity.

P1.text: Angular velocity, omega, is the angle turned each second, in radians per second.

P2.text: In a rigid body, every point turns the same angle in the same time. So all points share one omega.

P3.text: Omega is a vector along the axis. Curl your right fingers with the turn, and your thumb gives omega.

P4.text: Linear velocity, v, is how fast one point moves along its circle, in metres per second.

S1.text: To the motion notebook. The merry-go-round turns at zero point five radians per second. Omega points up.

S2.text: The inner horse is one metre from the pole. It moves at zero point five metres per second.

S3.text: The outer horse is three metres out. Same omega, but it moves at one point five. Three times faster.

S4.text: Now a marker walks out along the floor, from the pole to the edge.

S5.text: On the graph, its speed rises in a straight line. Double the distance from the axis, double the speed.

S6.text: Slow-mo replay. Freeze the outer horse.

S7.text: Draw r from a point O, low on the pole, to the horse: five metres, at angle theta to the pole.

S8.text: Its distance from the axis is r sine theta. Five times zero point six. Three metres.

S9.text: And v is at right angles to both omega and r, along the circle. So v equals omega cross r.

S10.text: Now you try. A point sits right on the pole. How fast does it move? Pause and decide.

S11.text: Zero! It is on the axis, so its distance from the axis is zero. It just turns on the spot.

D1.text: Now let's derive it, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. On a circle, arc length is radius times angle, with the angle in radians.

D3.text: Step two. Each second it turns omega radians, so the point moves omega times r perp. v equals omega r perp.

D4.text: Step three. With r from any point on the axis, r perp is r sine theta. So v is omega r sine theta.

D5.text: Step four. That is the size of a cross product. With direction, v equals omega cross r.

T1.text: Remember this. Every point shares one omega. Its speed is omega times its distance from the axis.

R1.text: Back to the two horses, link by link.

R2.text: Both horses finish a turn in the same time, about twelve point six seconds.

R3.text: In that turn, each goes once round its own circle. The outer circle is three times longer.

R4.text: Three times the distance in the same time: three times the speed.

K1.text: Side by side. Inner horse: one metre out, omega zero point five, v zero point five.

K2.text: Outer horse: three metres out, the same omega, but v is one point five.

K3.text: Now you try. The Earth turns once a day. Who moves faster: someone in Bengaluru, or in London? Pause and decide.

K4.text: Bengaluru! Same omega. But Bengaluru is nearer the equator, so it is farther from the Earth's axis.

W2.text: The Earth's radius is six point three seven times ten to the six metres. Find the speed on the equator, and in Bengaluru, thirteen degrees north.

W3.text: One turn a day: omega is two pi over eighty six thousand four hundred. About seven point two seven times ten to the minus five.

W4.text: On the equator, r perp is the full radius. v is about four hundred and sixty three metres per second.

W5.text: In Bengaluru, r perp is R cos thirteen, about six point two one times ten to the six metres.

W6.text: So v is about four hundred and fifty one metres per second, and we never feel it.

X2.text: Many students use the full distance r from the origin: v equals omega r.

X3.text: But only the distance from the axis counts. For our horse, omega r gives two point five. The truth is one point five.

E1.text: Where is this asked? v equals omega cross r, points on wheels and on the Earth, and rolling.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Omega is four k radians per second, about an axis through the origin. Find the speed of the point three i plus four j plus twelve k metres. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. Twenty metres per second.

A2.text: v is omega cross r. Four k cross three i is twelve j. Four k cross four j is minus sixteen i.

A3.text: So v is minus sixteen i plus twelve j. Its size is root of four hundred. Twenty.

A4.text: Check: r perp is five, and four times five is twenty. The twelve k does not count.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these without help?

Y2.text: One. Why do all points of a turning body share the same omega?

Y3.text: Two. Why does a point on the axis not move?

Y4.text: Three. Why use r sine theta, not r, in v equals omega r?

N1.text: Next time: a ceiling fan takes a few seconds to reach full speed. How many turns does it make on the way? Angular acceleration.
